I am sixty-three now, and I have worked these fields in Quzhou County since I was a young woman. I never went to school, but the land has been my teacher. My husband and I are the only ones left at home—our children work in the city and send money when they can, but I do not like to depend on them. We have eight mu of flat, irrigated land, and I know every corner of it.

This year, I will keep to what I know best: the wheat-maize double crop. In the autumn I will sow winter wheat, and after the harvest in early summer I will put in summer maize. I thought about planting cotton like some of my neighbors, but cotton means bending down to pick for weeks and spraying medicine more than ten times. My back is not strong enough for that anymore, and there is no one at home to help. Wheat and maize are easier—the machines can help with harvest, and the grain station buys them without fuss.

For the wheat, I will use Jimai 22, an improved seed that gives steady yields. I will rotary till the soil before sowing in early October. I will spread compound fertilizer as a base dressing and then top-dress with urea when the wheat greens up in spring. I will irrigate four times if the weather is dry: before winter dormancy, at green-up, at jointing, and during grain filling. I will spray for weeds and insects four times.

After the wheat comes off in June, I will sow Denghai 605 hybrid maize directly into the stubble without tilling. No-tillage saves time and keeps the soil moist in the summer heat. I will give it some fertilizer at sowing and a side-dressing when the stalks are knee-high. I will irrigate twice—once when the plants are growing fast and again when they tassel. I will spray pesticides three times to keep the armyworm and weeds away.

I expect about 1,000 jin per mu from the wheat and a little more from the maize. It is hard work, but it is honest work, and it is enough for us to live on.
